The word "mugger" has three distinct meanings. All three are in active use, though they appear in very different contexts. A thorough learner needs to know all three.
Meaning 1: A street robber (the most common meaning)

This is by far the most widely used meaning of "mugger" in everyday English.

A mugger is a person who attacks a stranger in a public place — such as a street, park, alley, subway station, or parking lot — with the goal of stealing their money, phone, jewellery, bag, or other valuables. The attack usually involves physical force, a threat, or a weapon. The mugger typically acts quickly and tries to escape before anyone intervenes.

The act itself is called a mugging.

Example sentences:

  • "She was walking home late at night when a mugger grabbed her purse and ran."
  • "The police arrested a mugger who had attacked three people near the train station."
  • "He had to be hospitalised after being beaten by a mugger."

How a mugger is different from similar criminals:

It helps to understand how a mugger differs from other types of criminals who steal:

  • A pickpocket steals from you secretly, without you knowing, without any confrontation or threat. A mugger, on the other hand, confronts you directly and openly. You know you're being robbed.
  • A burglar breaks into a building (your home, office, shop) to steal. A mugger attacks you in person, out in the open.
  • A thief is a general word for anyone who steals. A mugger is a specific type of thief — one who uses violence or intimidation against a person in a public place.

Key characteristics of a mugging:

  • It happens in a public or semi-public space, not inside a building.
  • The victim is a person (not a shop or a house).
  • There is direct confrontation — the mugger faces or approaches the victim.
  • Force, threats, or weapons are involved or implied.
Meaning 2: A type of crocodile (especially important if you live in South Asia)

A mugger (also written as muggar or muggur) is a species of crocodile — its full name is the mugger crocodile. It is scientifically known as Crocodylus palustris.

This crocodile is native to the Indian subcontinent and the surrounding region. It is found in India, Sri Lanka, Nepal, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Iran, and a few other nearby countries. It lives in freshwater environments — rivers, lakes, ponds, reservoirs, and marshes.

Characteristics of the mugger crocodile:

  • It is a medium-to-large-sized crocodile, typically growing between 2.5 to 4 metres in length, though some individuals can grow longer.
  • It has a broad, wide snout — wider than that of many other crocodile species. This is one of its most recognisable physical features.
  • It is considered an opportunistic predator, meaning it eats whatever prey is available — fish, frogs, birds, deer, and other animals that come close to the water.
  • It is known to be dangerous to humans and has been responsible for attacks, particularly in areas where it comes into close contact with human settlements near rivers and lakes.
  • It is classified as a vulnerable species, meaning its population is declining and it faces the risk of extinction if conditions do not improve. Habitat loss and hunting are the main threats.
  • In India, it is a protected animal under the Wildlife Protection Act.

Example sentences:

  • "Wildlife rangers spotted a mugger basking on the riverbank in the afternoon sun."
  • "The Chambal river in India is home to a significant population of mugger crocodiles."
  • "Conservationists are working to protect the mugger from habitat destruction."
Meaning 3: A person who "mugs" (makes exaggerated facial expressions)

This meaning is used primarily in the context of acting, theatre, film, and comedy.

When an actor or performer makes exaggerated, over-the-top, or comical facial expressions — pulling funny faces, widening their eyes dramatically, contorting their features for comedic effect, or playing to the audience in an exaggerated way — they are said to be "mugging". A person who does this habitually is called a mugger.

This is generally considered a somewhat negative term in professional acting circles. It implies that the actor is being too theatrical, too obvious, or too attention-seeking — prioritising laughs or audience attention over naturalistic, believable performance.

Example sentences:

  • "The director told the actor to stop mugging for the camera and deliver his lines more naturally."
  • "He was a natural mugger — every scene he was in, he'd pull faces that would make the audience roar with laughter."
  • "Silent film comedians like Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton were famous for their mugging."
How to tell which meaning is being used

Since all three meanings share the same word, context always makes it clear which one is intended:

  • If the sentence is about crime, theft, streets, or personal safety → it's the street robber.
  • If the sentence is about wildlife, rivers, reptiles, or conservation → it's the crocodile.
  • If the sentence is about acting, performance, comedy, or theatre → it's the expressive performer.

In practice, when you encounter "mugger" without any context, you should assume the street robber meaning, as it is the most common in everyday modern English.
